catalog_quote: Kikongo-Kituba has a predominantly fixed accent system, with the accent/tone borne by the penultimate syllable, as in any of its names. The majority of the words have only one accent (high tone) borne by the penultimate syllable (e.g. dísù HL ‘eye’, kwísà HL ‘come.IMP’, kàpítà LHL ‘foreman’, bábà HL ‘mute’). Derivative words and conjugated verbs are especially subject to this accent/tone placement rule, e.g. kù-sál-à LHL ‘to work’ ... kù-pés-à LHL ‘give’ > kù-pès-íl-à LLHL ‘give on the behalf, or for the benefit, of’. However, Kikongo-Kituba also has a significant proportion of polysyllabic words either with only low tones (e.g. mùntù LL ‘person’, mùnòkò LLL ‘mouth, opening’, dìkùlù LLL ‘leg, foot’, mbàlà LL ‘time’ as in ‘five times’) or with a high tone on the last syllable or on both the penultimate and last syllables (e.g. nzìlá LH ‘way, road’, mbàlá LH ‘yam’, dìlálá LHH ‘citrus frui…
sweep_summary: One bibliography item (Ngalasso 1991, Études Créoles 14(2): 147-162) — a dedicated 16-page first-hand study of the tone/accent question in exactly this variety (eastern Kituba of Bandundu, Zaire/DRC). Full text already downloaded by a the compilation (Persée PDF is altcha-gated; the 16 page scan and their scanned are; I read the whole scanned and verified the key passages against the page scan (pp. 148, 159, 160), and wrote. Ngalasso confirms the catalog's 'tonal' coding (the variety 'est toujours une langue à tons au sens le plus strict du terme', with minimal pairs and six lexical tonal schemes) and refines Mufwene 2013's 'accent/tone on the penultimate' statement: the canonical scheme I has H on the first root syllable (penult only in short words), other schemes are lexically contrastive, and an independent dynamic (length) accent falls on the first root syllable 'quel que soit le schème tonal', 'pas automatiquement sur la pénultième'; the penult-rise reading is called a superficial impression (while conceded for Brazzaville/Boma-Matadi broadcast speech). Best new statement: p. 159 'L'accent du kikongo' (quoted); it is a stronger first-hand source than the short APiCS survey chapter for the 'tonal' classification and adds a root-initial stress locus, so it can supersede or at least co-decide the record; catalog kind stays 'tonal'. The FSI Kituba Basic Course (Swift & Zola 1963, held by the project from the the compilation, not in the item list) states 'accent on the root syllable and pitch rise on the next to the last syllable' as the normal pattern (p. xv), consistent with Ngalasso. Nothing left to acquire for this item.

new_statements.quote: K. E. Laman (1936) l'avait déjà noté : l'énergie articulatoire caractéristique de l'accent dynamique du kikongo se localise en un point très précis à l'intérieur de l'unité lexicale : généralement sa place se trouve sur la première syllabe de la racine, quel que soit par ailleurs le schème tonal. Cette règle semble toujours en vigueur en kikongo véhiculaire. L'accent est particulièrement perceptible dans les formes prononcées avec une grande insistance : la voyelle accentuée a tendance à être prononcée plus longue que les autres. Les exemples qui suivent montrent clairement 1° que l'accent ne se confond pas systématiquement avec un ton haut ; 2° que sa place n'est pas automatiquement sur la pénultième.
new_statements.translation: K. E. Laman (1936) had already noted it: the articulatory energy characteristic of the dynamic accent of Kikongo is localised at a very precise point within the lexical unit: generally its place is on the first syllable of the root, whatever the tonal scheme. This rule seems still to be in force in vehicular Kikongo. The accent is particularly perceptible in forms pronounced with great insistence: the accented vowel tends to be pronounced longer than the others. The examples that follow show clearly 1° that the accent does not systematically coincide with a high tone; 2° that its place is not automatically on the penultimate syllable.
new_statements.citation: Ngalasso, Mwatha Musanji. 1991. Tons ou accents ? Analyse des schèmes tonals du kikongo parlé dans la région de Bandundu (Zaïre). Études Créoles 14(2): 147-162. doi:10.3406/ecreo.1991.1369
new_statements.locator: p. 159, section 'L'accent du kikongo', first paragraph (thesis restated p. 148 and in the Conclusion p. 160)
new_statements.reading: Eastern (Bandundu/DRC) Kituba keeps lexical tone (H/L + falling; minimal pairs; six lexical tonal schemes, of which the canonical scheme I puts H on the first root syllable, which is the penult only in di- and trisyllables) AND has an independent, non-contrastive dynamic accent (mainly length) fixed on the first syllable of the root/lexical base. The catalog's 'tonal' kind is confirmed; Mufwene's 'accent/tone borne by the penultimate syllable' is refined: the H of the canonical scheme is root-initial rather than penult-counting, other schemes (all-L, final-H, prefix-H, BHH) are lexically contrastive, and the stress proper is root-initial, not penultimate.

tone_statements.translation: [p.81] Phonologically, Kituba is mainly a fixed-tone language, the tone falling in most cases on the penultimate syllable. Urban Lingala, by contrast, is a heavily tonal language both lexically and grammatically. [p.87] One of the phonological characteristics that most distinguishes Kituba from ethnic Kikongo is that it has developed a system of phonological tones rather than grammatical or lexical ones as in Kikongo. [...] for the great majority of Kituba words the tone falls on the penultimate syllable, not forgetting the problem of the words [...] that have a tonal contour like that of their urban-Lingala cognates (illustrated in note 6).

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation and the exceptions quotation are verbatim in the held APiCS survey 58 text at the stated places (Section 3 Phonology, final paragraphs; Section 6 Closure). (2) Deciding source: a 2013 peer-reviewed survey sketch by the foremost Kituba specialist; short, but first-hand and tone-marked. (3) Better/other sources: the one dedicated prosody article (Ngalasso 1991, Études Créoles) and the 470-pp FSI course (Swift & Zola 1963) were both downloaded now into FSI pp. xv-xvi: default pattern = length-accent on root syllable plus pitch rise on the penult, with a lexical class of even/low-pitched (Lingala-cognate) words and French loans with non-penult pitch - the same picture as Mufwene. Ngalasso pp. 148-160: Kituba (Bandundu) remains a tone language with six lexical tone schemes; the penult-H scheme I is canoni

sources.note: The only dedicated study of Kituba word prosody; our record cites only a 10-page APiCS survey. It confirms lexical tone (six schemes, penult-H scheme I canonical, all-low and final-H classes) and adds that the length-accent is root-initial, not penult - worth adding as corroborating source and to sharpen the the primary-stress rule/the secondary-stress rule wording.
